learningObjectives.title: 14.1 Properties of Wave Pulses and Waves

questions.q: A string is stretched horizontally between two fixed supports, so the tension is the same all along it. It consists of two sections of equal length ℓ joined end to end, and section 2 has four times the mass of section 1. A pulse started at the support at the end of section 1 travels along section 1 at speed v. Which expression gives the time the pulse takes to reach the support at the far end of section 2?
optionWhy: A student who thinks a pulse travels faster on a string with more mass per length picks this: speed proportional to √(m/ℓ) gives 2v on section 2 and ℓ/v + ℓ/(2v) = 1.50ℓ/v. The speed is proportional to 1/√(m/ℓ), so the pulse slows to v/2 on section 2 and the total is 3.00ℓ/v.

A student who drops the square root, so that speed is inversely proportional to the mass per length, picks this: v/4 on section 2 gives ℓ/v + 4ℓ/v = 5.00ℓ/v. Speed depends on the square root, v = √(F_T/(m/ℓ)), so four times the mass per length halves the speed: 3.00ℓ/v.

A student who thinks the pulse keeps the speed it had on section 1, as a moving object would, picks this: 2ℓ/v = 2.00ℓ/v. The speed is set by the string the pulse is on: on section 2 it is v/2, so the total time is 3.00ℓ/v.
The tension is the same in both sections, and section 2 has four times the mass per length, so the pulse's speed there is v/√4 = v/2. The times add: ℓ/v + ℓ/(v/2) = 3.00ℓ/v.
questions.explain: The tension is the same in both sections, and section 2 has four times the mass per length, so the pulse's speed there is v/√4 = v/2. The times add: ℓ/v + ℓ/(v/2) = 3.00ℓ/v.
questions.working: Same tension and length; section 2 has four times the mass per length. v = √(F_T/(m/ℓ)), so v ∝ 1/√(m/ℓ) at fixed tension: v₂ = v/√4 = v/2. Times: t₁ = ℓ/v; t₂ = ℓ/(v/2) = 2ℓ/v. Total = 3.00ℓ/v. Errors: speed increasing with mass per length (v₂ = √4 v = 2v) gives ℓ/v + ℓ/(2v) = 1.50ℓ/v; square root dropped (v₂ = v/4) gives ℓ/v + 4ℓ/v = 5.00ℓ/v; speed v kept on section 2 gives 2.00ℓ/v.

questions.q: A uniform rope of mass m and length L hangs vertically from a ceiling, and a block of mass M hangs from its lower end. The rope's mass is not negligible, and g is the acceleration due to gravity. A small transverse pulse is started near the lower end and travels up the rope. Which expression gives the speed of the pulse just before it reaches the ceiling?
options: √(MgL/m)
√((M+m)gL/m)
√(ML/m)
optionWhy: A student who takes the tension to be Mg all along the rope, as for an ideal rope, picks this. Here the rope's own weight also hangs from the top point, so the tension there is (M + m)g and v = √((M + m)gL/m).

A student who uses the rope's whole mass m in place of its mass per length picks this. The speed depends on the mass per length, m/L, so v = √((M + m)g/(m/L)) = √((M + m)gL/m); this option does not even have the units of speed.
Just below the ceiling the rope holds up the block and all of the rope, so F_T = (M + m)g. With mass per length m/L, v = √(F_T/(m/L)) = √((M + m)gL/m).
A student who takes the tension to be the block's mass M, in kilograms, picks this. Tension is a force: at the top it equals the weight of everything hanging below, (M + m)g, so v = √((M + m)gL/m).
questions.explain: Just below the ceiling the rope holds up the block and all of the rope, so F_T = (M + m)g. With mass per length m/L, v = √(F_T/(m/L)) = √((M + m)gL/m).
questions.working: Just below the ceiling the rope supports the block and the whole rope: equilibrium of everything below that point gives F_T = Mg + mg = (M + m)g. Mass per length = m/L. v = √(F_T/(m/L)) = √((M + m)gL/m). (Lower down the tension is smaller, so the pulse speeds up as it rises.) Errors: tension Mg all along the rope gives √(MgL/m); whole mass m in place of m/L gives √((M + m)g/m); tension equal to the mass M gives √(ML/m).

questions.q: Each graph shows the air pressure P at a microphone as a function of time t for one of two sounds, X and Y. The two graphs are drawn to the same scale. P₀ is the pressure of the undisturbed air. Which statement about the two sounds is correct?
options: Y is louder, since its pressure changes more rapidly.
X travels through the air faster, as its amplitude is larger.
X is louder, since its pressure departs further from P₀.
Each is louder at the instants when its pressure is higher.
optionWhy: A student who links loudness to frequency picks this. Y's pressure does repeat more often, so Y has the higher frequency and the higher pitch, but pitch and loudness are different properties; loudness goes with amplitude, which is smaller for Y.

A student who thinks a sound of larger amplitude travels faster picks this. X does have the larger amplitude, but both sounds travel through the same air at the same speed; amplitude affects loudness, not speed.

The loudness of a sound increases with its amplitude, the maximum change in pressure from P₀. Sound X's pressure rises and falls about two gridlines from P₀, while Y's changes by less than one, so X has the larger amplitude and is louder.

A student who takes the pressure at one instant as the loudness picks this. The loudness of a steady sound depends on its amplitude, the maximum pressure change over a cycle, which is constant for each sound and larger for X.
questions.explain: The loudness of a sound increases with its amplitude, the maximum change in pressure from P₀. Sound X's pressure rises and falls about two gridlines from P₀, while Y's changes by less than one, so X has the larger amplitude and is louder.

figure.alt: Two graphs, one above the other, drawn to the same scale, each with P on the vertical axis and t on the horizontal axis and a horizontal line at P₀, with light gridlines equally spaced above and below P₀. The upper graph, labeled Sound X, shows a smooth wave whose pressure rises and falls two gridlines above and below P₀ and completes about three cycles across the graph. The lower graph, labeled Sound Y, shows a smooth wave whose pressure rises and falls less than one gridline from P₀ and completes about seven cycles across the graph.

questions.q: Two strings, 1 and 2, are under equal tension. At the same instant, a pulse is started at the left end (x = 0) of each string. The diagram shows the two strings at a later instant. How does the mass per length μ₁ of string 1 compare with the mass per length μ₂ of string 2?
options: μ₁ = 4μ₂, since speed is proportional to 1/√μ
μ₁ = 2μ₂, since speed is proportional to 1/μ
μ₂ = 4μ₁, since speed is proportional to √μ
μ₁ = μ₂, since the taller pulse travels faster
optionWhy: In the same time the pulse on string 2 has traveled 2.0 m and the pulse on string 1 only 1.0 m, so v₂ = 2v₁. With equal tensions, v = √(F_T/μ) gives μ = F_T/v², so μ₁/μ₂ = (v₂/v₁)² = 4.
A student who drops the square root, taking v ∝ 1/μ, picks this. Because v = √(F_T/μ), the mass per length goes as 1/v²: halving the speed means four times the mass per length.
A student who thinks a heavier string carries pulses faster picks this. The mass per length is in the denominator of v = √(F_T/μ): the slower string, string 1, has the larger mass per length.

A student who links the speed of a pulse to its amplitude picks this. The pulse on string 2 is taller, but amplitude does not affect the speed; with equal tensions, the only reason for the different speeds is a different mass per length.
questions.explain: In the same time the pulse on string 2 has traveled 2.0 m and the pulse on string 1 only 1.0 m, so v₂ = 2v₁. With equal tensions, v = √(F_T/μ) gives μ = F_T/v², so μ₁/μ₂ = (v₂/v₁)² = 4.
questions.working: Same time interval: Δx₁ = 1.0 m, Δx₂ = 2.0 m → v₂/v₁ = 2. v = √(F_T/μ), equal F_T → μ ∝ 1/v² → μ₁/μ₂ = (v₂/v₁)² = 4. Errors: v ∝ 1/μ → μ₁ = 2μ₂; v ∝ √μ → μ₂ = 4μ₁; amplitude explains speed → μ₁ = μ₂.

figure.alt: Diagram of two horizontal strings, String 1 above String 2, each fixed at the left at x = 0 and drawn over a common x (m) scale marked 0, 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0. String 1 has a small upward pulse centered at x = 1.0. String 2 has a taller upward pulse, about twice the height, centered at x = 2.0. Faint vertical lines mark x = 1.0 and x = 2.0.

questions.q: A car sounding its horn, whose rest frequency is f₀, moves along a straight road near a microphone that is at rest. The graph shows the frequency f measured by the microphone as a function of time t. Which claim is supported by the graph?
options: The car moved toward the microphone before t₁ and away from it after t₁.
The car moved away from the microphone before t₁ and toward it afterward.
The car kept approaching the microphone after t₁, but at a lower speed.
The car's horn itself was emitting a higher frequency before t₁ than after.
optionWhy: Before t₁ the measured frequency is above f₀, so the car and microphone were approaching each other; after t₁ it is below f₀, so they were moving apart. The frequency is steady on each side of t₁, consistent with a constant speed.

A student who links a higher frequency with a longer wavelength, and so with the stretched crests behind a receding source, picks this. A receding source gives a frequency below f₀; the graph is above f₀ before t₁, so the car was approaching then.

A student who thinks a drop in the observed frequency means the source slowed down picks this. A source that is still approaching, however slowly, gives a frequency above f₀; after t₁ the graph is below f₀, so the car was moving away.

A student who thinks a moving source changes the frequency it emits picks this. The horn emits f₀ throughout; the measured frequency changes because the car's velocity relative to the microphone changes from approaching to receding.
questions.explain: Before t₁ the measured frequency is above f₀, so the car and microphone were approaching each other; after t₁ it is below f₀, so they were moving apart. The frequency is steady on each side of t₁, consistent with a constant speed.

questions.q: The diagram shows a fire truck T sounding its siren, whose rest frequency is f₀, a car 1 and a person 2 beside a straight road; the velocity arrows are drawn to the same scale. The driver of car 1 hears frequency f₁ and person 2 hears frequency f₂. Which relationship is correct?
options: f₁ = f₂ < f₀
f₁ = f₂ = f₀
f₁ = f₀ < f₂
f₁ = f₀ > f₂
optionWhy: A student who thinks only the source's motion matters picks this: the truck is moving away from both, so both seem to hear a lower frequency. The driver of car 1 moves with the same velocity as the truck, so there is no relative velocity and no shift for that driver.

A student who thinks a moving siren changes only in loudness picks this. Person 2 is at rest while the siren moves away, so the crests reach person 2 less often than they are emitted and f₂ is less than f₀.

A student who thinks a longer wavelength means a higher frequency picks this: behind the receding truck the crests are spread out. Spread-out crests moving at the speed of sound reach person 2 less often, so f₂ is lower than f₀.

Car 1 moves with the same velocity as the truck, so it has no velocity relative to the siren and its driver hears the rest frequency. The truck is moving away from person 2, who is at rest, so person 2 hears a frequency lower than f₀.
questions.explain: Car 1 moves with the same velocity as the truck, so it has no velocity relative to the siren and its driver hears the rest frequency. The truck is moving away from person 2, who is at rest, so person 2 hears a frequency lower than f₀.
questions.working: Car 1 and T: same velocity → no relative velocity → f₁ = f₀. Person 2 at rest, T receding → f₂ < f₀.

questions.q: The diagram shows the crests of the sound waves from a source S that moves to the right at constant speed through still air. Listeners A and B are at rest. Listener A hears a higher frequency than listener B does. Which explanation, based on the diagram, is correct?
options: Crests are closer together on A's side of S, so they reach A more often.
The crests travel faster toward A, as the motion of S adds to their speed.
S emits a higher frequency toward A than toward B, since it moves toward A.
The sound reaching A is louder than at B, and a louder sound has a higher pitch.
optionWhy: Each crest spreads out at the speed of sound from the point where S was when it emitted that crest. Because S moves toward A, the crests on A's side are closer together; moving at the same speed, they pass A more often than they pass B, so A measures the higher frequency.

A student who thinks a moving source adds its velocity to its waves picks this. Every crest in the diagram is a circle, which shows that it spreads at the same speed in all directions through the air; what differs on the two sides is the spacing of the crests.

A student who thinks the source's motion changes the frequency it emits picks this. S emits one frequency, its rest frequency, in every direction; the circles are emitted at equal time intervals. The difference comes from where each crest starts, which changes how often crests reach each listener.

A student who thinks a louder sound has a higher pitch picks this. Loudness depends on amplitude and pitch on frequency; a louder sound is not a higher one. The diagram shows the reason A hears a higher frequency: the crests are more closely spaced on A's side.
questions.explain: Each crest spreads out at the speed of sound from the point where S was when it emitted that crest. Because S moves toward A, the crests on A's side are closer together; moving at the same speed, they pass A more often than they pass B, so A measures the higher frequency.

The circles are not centered on S: each larger circle is centered farther to the left, so on the right side of S the crests are close together and on the left side they are spread far apart. Listener A, a dot, is to the right of S and listener B, a dot, is to the left of S, at the same distance from S.

questions.q: Pipe X is open at both ends. The frequencies at which standing sound waves form in it are 400 Hz, 800 Hz, 1200 Hz, and so on. One end of pipe X is then closed, with its length and the air inside unchanged. What is now the second-lowest frequency at which a standing wave can form in the pipe?
optionWhy: Open at both ends, f_1 = v/(2L) = 400 Hz. With one end closed, the fundamental wavelength becomes 4L, so f_1 = v/(4L) = 200 Hz, and only odd harmonics can form: 200 Hz, 600 Hz, 1000 Hz, … The second-lowest is 600 Hz.

A student who thinks a pipe closed at one end has every harmonic, so that its second-lowest frequency is 2 × 200 Hz, picks this. With a node at one end and an antinode at the other, only odd harmonics form.

A student who thinks closing an end just removes the open pipe's even harmonics, leaving 400 Hz, 1200 Hz, …, picks this. Closing the end also doubles the fundamental wavelength to 4L, halving the fundamental to 200 Hz.
A student who thinks a pipe's standing-wave frequencies depend only on its length, so nothing changes, picks this. The end conditions matter too: a closed end must be a displacement node.
questions.explain: Open at both ends, f_1 = v/(2L) = 400 Hz. With one end closed, the fundamental wavelength becomes 4L, so f_1 = v/(4L) = 200 Hz, and only odd harmonics can form: 200 Hz, 600 Hz, 1000 Hz, … The second-lowest is 600 Hz.
questions.working: Open–open: f_1 = v/(2L) = 400 Hz, so v/L = 800 Hz. Closed–open: λ_1 = 4L, f_1 = v/(4L) = 200 Hz; odd harmonics only: 200, 600, 1000 Hz, … Second-lowest = 3 × 200 Hz = 600 Hz = 6.0 × 10² Hz.

questions.q: Three strings are each fixed at both ends and under the same tension. String 1 has length L and mass per length m/ℓ. String 2 has length L and mass per length 4(m/ℓ). String 3 has length L/2 and mass per length 4(m/ℓ). Which ranking of the frequencies f_1, f_2, and f_3 of their fundamental standing waves is correct?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the frequency depends only on the length, so that equal lengths give equal frequencies and the shorter string is higher, picks this. String 2's greater mass per length makes waves on it slower, which lowers its frequency.

A student who takes the wave speed to be inversely proportional to the mass per length, leaving out the square root, gets speeds v, v/4 and v/4, frequencies v/(2L), v/(8L) and v/(4L), and picks this. The speed depends on the square root: √4 = 2, not 4.

The fundamental wavelength is twice the length: 2L, 2L and L. The wave speed v = √(F_T/(m/ℓ)) is halved by four times the mass per length: v, v/2, v/2. So f = v/λ gives f_1 = v/(2L), f_2 = v/(4L) and f_3 = (v/2)/L = v/(2L).
A student who writes f = λv, making frequency grow with wavelength, gets 2Lv, Lv and Lv/2 and picks this. Frequency is v/λ: a shorter wavelength at the same speed means a higher frequency.
questions.explain: The fundamental wavelength is twice the length: 2L, 2L and L. The wave speed v = √(F_T/(m/ℓ)) is halved by four times the mass per length: v, v/2, v/2. So f = v/λ gives f_1 = v/(2L), f_2 = v/(4L) and f_3 = (v/2)/L = v/(2L).

questions.q: A student claims that point X on a string vibrating in a standing wave is a node. Which observation supports this claim?
options: A slow-motion video shows the string at X never moving away from equilibrium.
A single photograph of the vibrating string shows the string at X at equilibrium.
A slow-motion video shows the string at X moving farther from equilibrium than anywhere else.
X is the end of the string tied to a light ring that slides freely on a smooth rod.
optionWhy: A node is a point where the amplitude is always zero. Video over whole cycles showing that X never leaves equilibrium is exactly that evidence.

A student who thinks any point at equilibrium at one instant is a node picks this. Every point passes through equilibrium twice each cycle, and at some instants the whole string is straight; one photograph cannot show that X stays there.
A student who has node and antinode reversed picks this. A point that moves farther than any other is an antinode, the opposite of a node.

A student who thinks every end of a string is a node picks this. A loose end, free to slide on the rod, is an antinode: the string there moves more than anywhere else, so this observation counts against the claim.
questions.explain: A node is a point where the amplitude is always zero. Video over whole cycles showing that X never leaves equilibrium is exactly that evidence.

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in a standing wave. In the figure, the dashed curves show the extreme positions of the string, and the solid line shows the string at an instant when it is straight. Points J, K, and M are on the string. Which ranking of the speeds v_J, v_K, and v_M of these points at that instant is correct?
options: v_J = v_M = v_K = 0
v_J > v_M > v_K = 0
v_K > v_M > v_J = 0
v_J = v_M = v_K > 0
optionWhy: A student who thinks a point with zero displacement must be at rest picks this. The string is straight because every point is passing through equilibrium, which is where each moving point is fastest.

J is at an antinode, K at a node, and M between them, so their amplitudes rank J > M > K = 0. All points oscillate with the same period, and a point with a larger amplitude travels farther each cycle, so as the straight string passes through equilibrium J moves fastest, M more slowly, and K not at all.
A student who has the meanings of node and antinode reversed picks this. A node, like K, is where the amplitude is always zero; an antinode, like J, is where it is greatest.

A student who thinks every point on a standing wave oscillates with the same amplitude, as on a traveling wave, picks this. The amplitude varies along a standing wave, from zero at a node to a maximum at an antinode.
questions.explain: J is at an antinode, K at a node, and M between them, so their amplitudes rank J > M > K = 0. All points oscillate with the same period, and a point with a larger amplitude travels farther each cycle, so as the straight string passes through equilibrium J moves fastest, M more slowly, and K not at all.
questions.working: From the envelope: J is at an antinode (largest amplitude), K is at a node (amplitude zero), M is between a node and an antinode. At the straight instant every point is at equilibrium, moving at its greatest speed; with a common period, greatest speed increases with amplitude. So v_J > v_M > v_K = 0.

figure.alt: A string stretched horizontally between two walls. Two dashed curves show its extreme positions: they form three loops of equal length, meeting at the walls and crossing at two points between them. A solid straight horizontal line shows the string at the instant it is straight. Point J is at the middle of the first loop, where the dashed curves are farthest apart; point K is where the first and second loops meet, where the dashed curves cross; point M is in the third loop, halfway between the crossing point and the middle of that loop.

questions.q: Light of wavelength λ₁ passes through a narrow slit and forms a diffraction pattern on a distant screen, where the central bright band has width W. The light is then replaced by light of wavelength λ₂, with the slit and the screen unchanged, and the fourth-order dark band is now a distance W from the middle of the central bright band. Assume small angles. Which expression gives λ₂?
optionWhy: With λ₁ the first dark bands are at λ₁L/a on each side of the middle, so W = 2λ₁L/a. With λ₂ the fourth-order dark band is at 4λ₂L/a. Setting 4λ₂L/a = 2λ₁L/a gives λ₂ = 0.50λ₁.

A student who takes the full width of the central bright band as the distance y_min to the first dark band sets W = λ₁L/a, gets 4λ₂ = λ₁, and picks this. The first dark bands are on both sides of the middle, each λ₁L/a away, so the central band's width is 2λ₁L/a.

A student who puts the dark bands where the path length difference is (m − ½)λ gets W = λ₁L/a and places the fourth-order dark band at (7/2)λ₂L/a, so λ₂ = (2/7)λ₁ ≈ 0.29λ₁. For a single slit the dark bands are where a sin θ = mλ, so y_min = mλL/a.

A student who thinks shorter wavelengths spread out more treats the band positions as inversely proportional to the wavelength, sets 4/λ₂ = 2/λ₁, and picks this. The positions are proportional to the wavelength, y_min = mλL/a, so the fourth-order band reaches W only when λ₂ is half of λ₁.
questions.explain: With λ₁ the first dark bands are at λ₁L/a on each side of the middle, so W = 2λ₁L/a. With λ₂ the fourth-order dark band is at 4λ₂L/a. Setting 4λ₂L/a = 2λ₁L/a gives λ₂ = 0.50λ₁.
questions.working: Small angles: a(y_min/L) ≈ mλ, so y_min = mλL/a. With λ₁ the first-order dark bands lie at ±λ₁L/a, so W = 2λ₁L/a. With λ₂ the fourth-order dark band is at 4λ₂L/a. Setting 4λ₂L/a = 2λ₁L/a gives λ₂ = λ₁/2 = 0.50λ₁.

questions.q: Light from the same laser passes through two different narrow openings, one at a time, and falls on a screen at the same distance. The figure shows graphs of the intensity of the resulting patterns X and Y as a function of position y on the screen, each scaled so that its central peak has the same height. Which claim is supported by the graphs?
options: The opening for X is wider than the opening used for Y.
The openings are equally wide, as the same laser was used.
Pattern Y came from two slits, as its maxima are closer.
The opening for X is narrower than the opening for Y.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the central band is an image of the opening picks this. The wider central peak comes from the narrower opening: a is in the denominator of y_min ≈ λL/a.

A student who thinks the pattern is set by the light alone picks this. With the same wavelength and screen distance, the only way to get central peaks of different widths is openings of different widths.

A student who takes closely spaced bands as the sign of two slits picks this. Pattern Y has the same shape as X, a central peak twice as wide as its much weaker side peaks, which is the pattern of a single opening. Its bands are closer together only because its opening is wider.

Both patterns are single-slit patterns (one wide central peak with much weaker side peaks). The first zeros of X are at ±6 mm and those of Y at ±3 mm. With λ and L the same, y_min ≈ λL/a, so X's opening is narrower, half as wide as Y's.
questions.explain: Both patterns are single-slit patterns (one wide central peak with much weaker side peaks). The first zeros of X are at ±6 mm and those of Y at ±3 mm. With λ and L the same, y_min ≈ λL/a, so X's opening is narrower, half as wide as Y's.
questions.working: X: zeros at ±6 mm; Y: zeros at ±3 mm. y_min ∝ 1/a (same λ, L) → a_X = a_Y/2: X's opening is narrower.

figure.alt: Two graphs of intensity against position, one above the other, sharing a horizontal axis labeled y (mm) and marked −18, −12, −6, 0, 6, 12 and 18. The upper graph, labeled Pattern X, has a central peak at 0 that falls to zero at −6 and 6, with small side peaks beyond. The lower graph, labeled Pattern Y, has a central peak of the same height that falls to zero at −3 and 3, with small side peaks and zeros every 3 mm beyond. Both central peaks are drawn with the same height.

questions.q: In a single-slit experiment, the first dark band is 4.00 mm from the middle of the central bright band. The laser is replaced by one whose light has half the wavelength, and the slit is replaced by one half as wide. The screen is not moved. How far from the middle of the central bright band is the first dark band now?
optionWhy: A student who thinks a narrower slit gives a narrower pattern picks this, treating y_min as proportional to both λ and a: (1/2)(1/2) × 4.00 mm = 1.00 mm. The slit width is in the denominator of y_min ≈ mλL/a, so halving a doubles y_min.

A student who thinks shorter-wavelength light spreads more picks this, treating y_min as inversely proportional to both λ and a: 2 × 2 × 4.00 mm = 16.0 mm. y_min is proportional to λ, so halving the wavelength halves y_min.

A student who thinks the spreading depends only on the light, not on the slit, picks this, halving y_min for the halved wavelength and ignoring the narrower slit. Halving a doubles y_min, which cancels the effect of halving λ.
y_min ≈ mλL/a. Halving λ halves y_min, and halving a doubles it, so the two changes cancel: y_min stays 4.00 mm.
questions.explain: y_min ≈ mλL/a. Halving λ halves y_min, and halving a doubles it, so the two changes cancel: y_min stays 4.00 mm.

questions.q: A lamp emits only blue light of wavelength 450 nm and red light of wavelength 650 nm. The light passes through a diffraction grating. The figure shows the central maximum C and the three bright lines nearest to it on one side of the pattern, J, K and L. Which line is the first-order maximum of the red light?
options: Line J, the nearest to C
Line K, between J and L
Line L, the farthest from C
C, the central maximum
optionWhy: A student who thinks shorter wavelengths are deflected more picks this, expecting red to be nearest. d sin θ = λ puts the 450 nm first-order line at the smallest angle, so J is blue.
The lines appear in order of increasing mλ: 450 nm (blue, first order) at J, 650 nm (red, first order) at K, and 2 × 450 nm = 900 nm (blue, second order) at L. The red first-order line is K.
A student who treats every line as first order picks this, expecting red to be farthest. L is the second-order blue line, where mλ = 900 nm, which is more than the 650 nm of the red first-order line.

A student who counts the central maximum as the first-order maximum picks this. C is the zeroth-order maximum (m = 0), where every wavelength arrives in step; the first-order red maximum is where d sin θ = 650 nm.
questions.explain: The lines appear in order of increasing mλ: 450 nm (blue, first order) at J, 650 nm (red, first order) at K, and 2 × 450 nm = 900 nm (blue, second order) at L. The red first-order line is K.
questions.working: Lines in order of mλ: 450 nm (m = 1, blue) → J; 650 nm (m = 1, red) → K; 900 nm (m = 2, blue) → L; next 1300 nm (m = 2, red), not shown. Figure drawn for d = 2.0 μm, L = 1.0 m: y = 0.23 m, 0.34 m, 0.50 m.

figure.alt: Diagram of a screen (one side of the pattern): a horizontal line with a thick bright line C at its left end, the central maximum, and three thinner bright lines to the right of C, labelled J, K and L in order of increasing distance from C. The distances from C to J, K and L are in the ratio of about 23 : 34 : 50.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through two narrow slits onto a screen 2.0 m away. The graph shows the intensity I of the light on the screen against position y, measured from the center of the pattern. What is the separation of the slits?
optionWhy: The maxima are 3.0 mm apart, so the first-order maximum is at y_max = 3.0 mm. d = mλL/y_max = (1)(600 × 10⁻⁹ m)(2.0 m)/(3.0 × 10⁻³ m) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.40 mm.
A student who uses the outermost maximum shown, at 9.0 mm, as if it were first order picks this. That maximum is third order; with m = 3, d = 3λL/y = 0.40 mm.
A student who uses the 6.0 mm between the first-order maxima on opposite sides as y_max picks this. y_max for the first-order maximum is measured from the center: 3.0 mm.
A student who thinks ΔD = λ at a minimum picks this, using the first minimum, at 1.5 mm, as if it were the first-order position. At that minimum ΔD = λ/2; the first-order maximum is at 3.0 mm.
questions.explain: The maxima are 3.0 mm apart, so the first-order maximum is at y_max = 3.0 mm. d = mλL/y_max = (1)(600 × 10⁻⁹ m)(2.0 m)/(3.0 × 10⁻³ m) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.40 mm.
questions.working: From the graph, maxima at y = 0, ±3.0, ±6.0, ±9.0 mm; minima halfway between (±1.5 mm, …). First order: y_max = 3.0 mm. d = mλL/y_max = (600 × 10⁻⁹ m)(2.0 m)/(3.0 × 10⁻³ m) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.40 mm. Largest angle shown: 9.0 mm/2.0 m ≈ 0.26°, so the small-angle relation applies.

figure.alt: Graph of intensity I (vertical axis) against y (mm) (horizontal axis). The horizontal axis is marked −9, −6, −3, 0, 3, 6 and 9. The curve has peaks of equal height at y = 0 and at every mark, −9 to 9, and falls to zero halfway between neighboring marks. The pattern continues just beyond −9 and 9.

questions.q: The graph shows the intensity I of light on a screen against position y for monochromatic light passing through two identical narrow slits. The dashed curve is the envelope within which the bright peaks lie. One of the slits is then covered. Which statement describes the new pattern?
options: The narrow peaks vanish, leaving the envelope's shape: one broad peak and faint side peaks.
The same narrow peaks stay in the same places, each one becoming less intense.
A single narrow peak remains, located directly in line with the open slit.
The whole pattern shrinks to half its width, as half the opening is now blocked.
optionWhy: With one slit covered there is no second wave to interfere with, so the evenly spaced narrow peaks disappear. What remains is the diffraction pattern of the open slit, which has the shape of the envelope: one broad central peak, as wide as the envelope's central region, with faint peaks beyond it.

A student who thinks the second slit only makes the same pattern brighter picks this: covering it should just dim every peak. The narrow peaks come from interference between the waves from the two slits, so they cannot survive when one slit is covered.
A student who thinks light goes straight through a slit picks this. The open slit is narrow, so its light still spreads out, giving a broad peak as wide as the envelope's central region.

A student who thinks less opening gives a narrower beam picks this. Covering one slit does not make the remaining slit any narrower, so its light spreads just as much; the broad envelope stays the same width while the narrow peaks disappear.
questions.explain: With one slit covered there is no second wave to interfere with, so the evenly spaced narrow peaks disappear. What remains is the diffraction pattern of the open slit, which has the shape of the envelope: one broad central peak, as wide as the envelope's central region, with faint peaks beyond it.

figure.alt: Graph of intensity I (vertical axis) against position y (horizontal axis), with y = 0 at the center. A solid curve shows many narrow, evenly spaced peaks. The central peak is the tallest; the peaks become lower on either side and reach zero height at the fourth peak position on each side, beyond which a few much lower peaks appear. A dashed curve labelled 'dashed: envelope' passes over the tops of the peaks: a broad central hump that falls to zero at those points and then rises into small side humps.

questions.q: A soap film (n = 1.33) in air is lit at normal incidence by green light of wavelength 532 nm in air. Two regions of the film have thicknesses of 100 nm and 200 nm. Which comparison of the light reflected from the two regions, with its reasoning, is correct?
options: Brighter at 100 nm, where the film has less pigment to absorb the green
Brighter at 200 nm, where the path difference is one wavelength in the film
Brighter at 200 nm, where the thicker film reflects more of the light
Brighter at 100 nm, where the two reflected waves arrive in phase
optionWhy: A student who thinks a film's color and brightness come from pigments absorbing light picks this. Soap film has no pigment and absorbs almost no light at either thickness; the difference comes from interference of the two reflected waves, which are in phase at 100 nm and out of phase at 200 nm.

A student who uses the path difference alone picks this. The path difference at 200 nm is one wavelength in the film, but one reflection changes phase by 180°, so the waves there are out of phase and the reflection is weak.

A student who thinks a thicker film reflects more light picks this. Brightness depends on the phase difference between the two reflected waves; at 200 nm they are out of phase and the reflection is weak.

In the film λ/n = 532 nm/1.33 = 400 nm. At 100 nm the path difference 2t = 200 nm is half a wavelength, which with the single 180° change at the top surface puts the waves in phase: strong reflection. At 200 nm, 2t = 400 nm is one whole wavelength, so the single 180° change leaves the waves out of phase: weak reflection.
questions.explain: In the film λ/n = 532 nm/1.33 = 400 nm. At 100 nm the path difference 2t = 200 nm is half a wavelength, which with the single 180° change at the top surface puts the waves in phase: strong reflection. At 200 nm, 2t = 400 nm is one whole wavelength, so the single 180° change leaves the waves out of phase: weak reflection.
questions.working: λ_film = 532 nm/1.33 = 400 nm. One 180° change (top surface only). t = 100 nm: 2t = 200 nm = λ_film/2, plus the 180° change → in phase (constructive). t = 200 nm: 2t = 400 nm = λ_film, plus the 180° change → 180° out of phase (destructive).

questions.q: Camera lenses with an antireflection coating designed to eliminate the reflection of green light (about 550 nm) look faintly purple when white light reflects from them. Which reasoning explains the purple color?
options: The coating absorbs green light, so the light that it reflects contains no green light.
Reflection is canceled best for green, so some red and blue light is still reflected.
The coating spreads white light into its colors like a prism and reflects the purple part.
The coating scatters green light off to the sides, so less green reaches the eye.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the coating works by absorbing light picks this. The coating is transparent; the green light that is not reflected is transmitted into the lens.

The coating's thickness gives exactly half a wavelength of path difference only for green light. For red and blue light the two reflected waves are not exactly 180° out of phase, so they cancel only partly, and a mixture of red and blue, which looks purple, is reflected.

A student who explains colors from thin layers by dispersion picks this. The coating is flat and thin; the color comes from interference, which cancels the reflection of some wavelengths more than others.
A student who thinks the coating works like a matte finish picks this. The coating is smooth; less green light is reflected because the two reflected green waves interfere destructively.
questions.explain: The coating's thickness gives exactly half a wavelength of path difference only for green light. For red and blue light the two reflected waves are not exactly 180° out of phase, so they cancel only partly, and a mixture of red and blue, which looks purple, is reflected.

questions.q: A vertical soap film in a wire loop is lit by white light. The diagram shows the film from the side and from the front, where horizontal bands of different colors are seen. Which explanation of the bands is supported by the diagram?
options: The film's thickness changes with height, so the wavelength reflected most strongly changes too.
The film acts like a prism, spreading the colors of white light out from its top down to its bottom.
Dye in the soap drains downward, so each height absorbs a different part of the white light.
Thicker parts of the film reflect more light, so each band is brighter than the band above it.
optionWhy: The side view shows that the film gets thicker from top to bottom. At each height, the wavelengths that interfere constructively depend on the thickness there, so each height reflects a different color, and the bands run horizontally, along lines of equal thickness.

A student who explains thin-film colors by dispersion picks this. The film's colors come from interference of light reflected from its two surfaces; the side view shows the thickness changing with height, which is what sets the color.

A student who thinks the colors come from dyes picks this. Clear soap solution gives the same bands; the diagram's side view shows the thickness changing with height, and the thickness sets which wavelengths interfere constructively.

A student who thinks thicker films reflect more light picks this. The front view shows repeating bands of different colors, not a steady brightening downward; reflection rises and falls with thickness because of interference.
questions.explain: The side view shows that the film gets thicker from top to bottom. At each height, the wavelengths that interfere constructively depend on the thickness there, so each height reflects a different color, and the bands run horizontally, along lines of equal thickness.
